entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Detroit, Wayne County, Michigan (1870–1930)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Wayne County organized November 21, 1815; Detroit established as county seat well before statehood
- **County seat:** Detroit
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Michigan (state since 1837)
- **Population during period:** 119,068 (1870) → 168,444 (1880) → 348,793 (1900) → 531,591 (1910) → 1,177,645 (1920) → 1,888,946 (1930) — explosive industrial growth driven by automotive industry from ~1900
- **Economy:** Heavy manufacturing, automotive industry (Ford, GM, Chrysler from ~1900), river commerce, metalworking, brewing
- **Ethnic composition:** Large Irish, German, Polish, Italian, Eastern European, and African American communities; Irish immigration peaked 1845–1880
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (Archdiocese of Detroit, very large Irish/German/Polish parishes), Lutheran, Methodist, Baptist, Episcopal, Presbyterian
- **Key historical events:** Industrial boom 1900s–1920s; WWI and WWII mobilization; automobile manufacturing explosion; Great Migration of African Americans 1910–1930

## Boundary changes
- Wayne County boundaries have been stable since the 19th century; no significant county-level boundary changes during 1870–1930
- Detroit itself expanded dramatically through annexations 1806–1926, especially 1915–1925 — many surrounding community names (Delray, Hamtramck, Highland Park) were absorbed or became distinct municipalities; confirm which jurisdiction your subject was in for any given year

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Statewide registration of births and deaths began 1867; general compliance by 1915. Marriage records from 1833 (Wayne County)
- **CRITICAL SPLIT:** Wayne County civil vital records divide into two streams:
  - **City of Detroit births** (since 1893) and **deaths** (since 1897): held at the Wayne County Clerk's Office, Coleman A. Young Municipal Center, Detroit. FamilySearch's unindexed Wayne County birth/death films (1867–1917) do NOT cover City of Detroit — search the indexed collections instead.
  - **Rest of Wayne County births/deaths** (1867–1917): FamilySearch unindexed microfilm; also covered in indexed collections below.
- **FamilySearch indexed births:** Michigan, Births, 1867-1902 (coll. 1459684) — indexed + images; Michigan, County Births, 1867-1917 (coll. 1923472) — indexed + images
- **FamilySearch indexed marriages:** Michigan, County Marriages, 1820-1941 (coll. 1810350) — indexed + images; Michigan, Marriages, 1868-1925 (coll. 1452395) — indexed + images
- **FamilySearch indexed deaths:** Michigan, Deaths, 1867-1897 (coll. 1452402) — indexed + images; Michigan, Death Certificates, 1921-1952 (coll. 1968532) — index only (images at Michiganology / Ancestry)
- **Ancestry:** Michigan Death Records 1867-1952 (coll. michigandeaths) — indexed + images ($); Michigan Marriage Records 1867-1952 (coll. 9093) ($)
- **Wayne County Death Index 1934–1953** (non-Detroit only): Burton Historical Collection, Detroit Public Library
- **Gaps:** No statewide birth/death registration before 1867; pre-1867 records are church records only

### Church records
- **Most important for Mogan/McAndrew (Irish Catholic):** Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Detroit records, 1704–1930, available on microfilm at the **Burton Historical Collection, Detroit Public Library** — includes baptisms, marriages, deaths, first communions, and confirmations. This is the single most important repository for Irish Catholic families in Detroit.
- **FamilySearch:** Michigan, Church Records, 1819-1991 (coll. 2787825) — 33K records, indexed + images; Michigan, Church Marriages, 1865-1931 (coll. 2515887) — 213 records
- **Lutheran:** American Lutheran Church Detroit-area records in ELCA database at Archives.com ($)
- **Language:** English for most 19th–20th century Detroit Catholic records

### Census records
- **Federal census years available:** 1870, 1880, 1900, 1910, 1920, 1930 — all indexed at FamilySearch and Ancestry; 97% record-searchable for Detroit area volumes per volume_search
- **1890 DESTROYED:** The 1890 federal census was almost entirely destroyed by fire — no Wayne County 1890 census exists. Bridge this gap with the 1894 Michigan State Census, city directories, and vital records.
- **1894 Michigan State Census:** FamilySearch coll. 1825187, index only (Civil War veterans); also Ancestry ($)
- **Relationship to head of household** added in 1880 census — 1880 and later censuses directly enumerate all household members' relationships
- **Street renumbering:** Detroit renumbered all streets on 1 January 1921. A family at the same address will appear under different numbers in 1920 vs. 1930 census.

### Probate and court records
- **Wayne County probate 1832–1967:** FamilySearch coll. 2013878 — **browse-only images** (4.7M images, 0% name-indexed). Use Ancestry's indexed Michigan Wills and Probate 1784-1980 (coll. 8793) ($) or FamilySearch full-text search for access.
- **Wayne County estate case files 1797–1901:** Archives of Michigan, Lansing; probate calendar books 1797–1914 also at Archives of Michigan
- **Burton Historical Collection** at Detroit Public Library holds estate packets 1797–1901
- Probate records frequently name all surviving children and their spouses — high-value source for completeness questions

### Land records
- **System:** Federal rectangular survey (Michigan is a public-land state)
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages at Wayne County Register of Deeds (waynecountylandrecords.com)
- **FamilySearch:** Michigan, Wills and Deeds, ca. 1700s-2017 (coll. 3158869) — limited indexed records but images available

### Military records
- **WWI draft registrations (1917-1918):** Available nationwide at FamilySearch and Ancestry — all men born 1872-1900 registered; will list address and next of kin
- **WWII draft (1940):** Michigan, World War II Draft Registration Cards (FamilySearch coll. 2999489)
- **Michigan, Census of World War I Veterans, 1917-1919** (FamilySearch coll. 3007553) — 227K records

### Cemetery records
- **Major Detroit cemeteries:** Elmwood Cemetery (1846-1992 records at Burton Historical Collection), Mt. Elliot Cemetery (1845-1997), Woodmere Cemetery (1868+), Detroit City Cemetery (1854-1861)
- **Online:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com) and BillionGraves — good Wayne County coverage
- **Burton Historical Collection** at Detroit Public Library holds sexton records for multiple Detroit cemeteries

### Newspaper records
- **Detroit Free Press and Detroit News** — major dailies throughout the period; obituaries name all surviving children
- **Chronicling America** (loc.gov): Michigan digitized newspapers free online
- **Ancestry:** Michigan Newspapers via Newspapers.com ($); GenealogyBank ($)
- **Michigan Obituaries 1820-2006** at FamilySearch (coll. 2215693) — 8.9M records, indexed + images — extremely high-value for completeness research; obituaries routinely list all surviving children by name and often married surnames

### Directories
- **Detroit City Directories 1861-1923:** Fold3 ($); also Hathi Trust for Michigan State Gazetteers and Business Directories 1863-1922 (free)
- **US City Directories at Ancestry** (coll. 1540) — useful for locating family year-by-year between censuses
- City directories will show annual household composition changes and can reveal adult children who moved out or married

### Immigration/naturalization records
- **Michigan Naturalization Records, 1837-1997** (FamilySearch coll. 2546149) — 2.1M records, indexed + images
- **Michigan Eastern District Naturalization Index, 1907-1995** (FamilySearch coll. 2110745) — 567K records
- **Detroit Port Manifests, 1906-1956** (FamilySearch coll. 1916040) — 1.36M records; covers arrivals at Port of Detroit from Canada

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Key collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Births 1867-1917, Marriages 1820-1941, Deaths 1867-1897 + 1921-1952, Probate 1797-1973 (images), Obituaries 1820-2006, Church Records 1819-1991, Census all years, Naturalization | Free |
| Ancestry | Michigan Deaths 1867-1952, Marriages 1867-1952, Probate 1784-1980, Newspapers, City Directories, Naturalization | Subscription ($) |
| Michiganology (michiganology.org) | Death Certificates 1897-1952 organized by county/name | Free |
| Chronicling America (LOC) | Michigan newspapers | Free |

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Burton Historical Collection, Detroit Public Library | Catholic Archdiocese microfilms 1704-1930; Wayne County marriage returns 1803-1893; cemetery records (Elmwood, Mt. Elliot, etc.); Wayne County Death Index 1934-1953 | In-person; some by mail |
| Wayne County Clerk's Office, Detroit | Birth records (City of Detroit since 1893), death records (since 1897), marriage/divorce records | In-person/mail |
| Archives of Michigan, Lansing | Wayne County estate case files 1797-1901; probate calendar books 1797-1914 | In-person/online request |
| Archdiocese of Detroit Archives | Parish registers not yet microfilmed | Contact for access |

## Records NOT online
- City of Detroit birth certificates before ~1893 — contact Wayne County Clerk directly
- Detroit Catholic parish registers not covered by Burton microfilms
- Wayne County probate packets in full (only calendar/index at FamilySearch; full packets at Archives of Michigan)
- Pre-1867 vital records not captured in church records

## Known record losses
- **1890 federal census**: Almost entirely destroyed by fire nationwide — no substitute exists for the specific enumeration, but the 1894 Michigan State Census partially fills this gap
- No known major courthouse fires for Wayne County

## Research tips
- **Irish Catholic families (Mogan/McAndrew):** Begin with Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Detroit baptism registers at Burton Historical Collection — these capture children not reached by civil registration before 1915 compliance.
- **Obituaries are essential for completeness:** Michigan Obituaries at FamilySearch (coll. 2215693) frequently lists all surviving children by name; search obituaries for both parents AND each known child.
- **Probate is a completeness workhorse:** John Mogan's probate (if he predeceased Mary) or Mary's probate should name all surviving children as heirs. Search Ancestry's indexed Michigan probate (coll. 8793) first, then browse FamilySearch images.
- **Search all census years 1870-1930** for the family household: 1870, 1880, 1900, 1910, 1920, 1930 (remember 1890 is lost). Children living at home across these enumerations will enumerate the family incrementally.
- **Death certificates of known children** (Michigan, Death Certificates 1921-1952 at FamilySearch coll. 1968532; Ancestry 1867-1952) name parents — confirm parentage and may mention siblings.
- **Marriage records of known children** list parents' names — search Michigan County Marriages 1820-1941.
- **Detroit street renumbering (1 Jan 1921):** When comparing 1920 and 1930 census entries at the same address, the street numbers will differ.
- **Consult the FamilySearch Wiki article 'Wayne County, Michigan Genealogy'** for additional record-type specific links.

entry.rationale: Federal censuses of 1880, 1900, 1910, 1920, and 1930 are the primary household-enumeration records. The 1880 census introduced relationship-to-head columns. The 1900 and 1910 censuses include mother's number of children born and number still living — the single most direct evidence for a completeness question. Searching all available years identifies children living at home at each snapshot and may surface children not yet in the tree. Note: the 1890 federal census is destroyed nationally; see pli_002 for the Michigan state census bridge.

The 1894 Michigan State Census (FamilySearch coll. 1825187, 381K records, indexed) bridges the 14-year gap left by the destroyed 1890 federal census. It may capture children who appear between 1880 and 1900, including adolescents who had left home by 1900, and children born in the late 1880s who would otherwise not appear in any household record until 1900.

Search Michigan Births, 1867-1902 (coll. 1459684, 1.4M records, indexed + images) and Michigan County Births, 1867-1917 (coll. 1923472, 724K records, indexed + images) for all births registered under surname Mogan (and variants: Morgan, Mogan, Magan) in Wayne County. Per the locality guide, these indexed collections DO include City of Detroit records, unlike the unindexed FamilySearch microfilm which excludes Detroit. Birth certificates capture all registered children including those who died in infancy before appearing in any census.

Children who died in infancy or childhood will not appear in census household records but will have registered deaths. Search Michigan Deaths, 1867-1897 (coll. 1452402, 507K records, indexed + images) and Michigan Death Certificates, 1921-1952 (coll. 1968532, 1.65M records, index only at FS; images at Michiganology/Ancestry) for Mogan surname deaths in Wayne County. Death certificates from 1897 onward name parents, confirming parentage and revealing children who survived only briefly.

Michigan Obituaries 1820-2006 (FamilySearch coll. 2215693, 8.9M records, indexed + images) draws from Detroit newspapers. Obituaries for John Mogan, Mary McAndrew/Mogan, and each known child routinely list all surviving children by name, often including married surnames for daughters — the most family-knowledge-rich source for a completeness question. Search all names: both parents and all currently known children. A parent's obituary is the single most likely record to enumerate every child.

A will or estate administration for John Mogan or Mary McAndrew would name all surviving children as heirs — the most definitive enumeration for a completeness question. Search Ancestry's indexed Michigan, U.S., Wills and Probate Records, 1784-1980 (coll. 8793, index + images) for both names. If John predeceased Mary, her probate is equally important. Wayne County probate jurisdiction is confirmed in the locality guide; the Probate Court is at Coleman A. Young Municipal Center, Detroit.

Fallback if Ancestry's indexed probate yields nothing. FamilySearch Michigan Probate Records, 1797-1973 (coll. 2013878, 4.7M browse-only images) covers Wayne County. Access via the FamilySearch full-text search interface rather than browsing image-by-image, as the collection is 0% name-indexed. The Archives of Michigan (Lansing) also holds Wayne County estate case files 1797-1901 as a physical fallback.

Each known child's marriage record names both parents and confirms parentage. Search Michigan County Marriages, 1820-1941 (coll. 1810350, 498K records, indexed + images) and Michigan Marriages, 1868-1925 (coll. 1452395, 1.6M records) for each currently known child: Anna Irene Mogan, Bernard McAndrews, Edward Lawrence Mogan, Abby [Mogan], Thomas Frank Mogan, John Vincent Mogan, Mary L. Mogan. Witness names on marriage records are a FAN cluster source and may surface siblings not yet in the tree.

Mogan and McAndrew are Irish surnames, indicating a likely Roman Catholic family. Catholic Archdiocese of Detroit baptismal registers (1704-1930) are available on microfilm at the Burton Historical Collection, Detroit Public Library. Church baptisms are the most comprehensive source for an Irish Catholic family's children — they predate consistent civil-registration compliance (not fully achieved until 1915) and capture children who died before being registered civilly. Contact: Burton Historical Collection, Detroit Public Library. Also search FamilySearch Michigan Church Records, 1819-1991 (coll. 2787825) as a preliminary indexed check.

Detroit City Directories (1861-1923, available at Fold3/Ancestry; Michigan State Gazetteers and Business Directories 1863-1922 at HathiTrust, free) provide annual household snapshots between census years. Adult children who moved out before a census enumeration year appear at separate Detroit addresses. Cross-referencing the family's address across multiple directory years reveals children who had established independent households. Per locality guide, note Detroit street renumbering on 1 January 1921 — pre- and post-1921 addresses for the same house will differ.

Same surname Mogan, same birth date and place as tree person. Primary source (presenting parents). No same_person score obtained (tree person lacks resolvable ARK for FS scoring). Birth date conflict noted (tree: 1879 vs this record: 1877) — birth record is the authoritative primary source.
Sex assertion (Male) from same birth record; confirmed as part of the 9XPJ-TRP persona.

Relationship assertion: John V Mogan is child of John Mogan (father). Links to 9XPJ-TRP as the child party.
Relationship assertion: child of John Mogan. Links to GQWY-3JF as the father. Father named 'John Mogan', born Ireland — exact name and birthplace match to tree person GQWY-3JF.

exhaustive_declaration.justification: The 1900 US Census directly states Mary E. Mogan was mother of 7 children born (4 living at enumeration), proving at least 7 total children against the tree's original 5 (log_002). Three Michigan death certificates independently confirm Frank, John Vincent, and Ed Mogan as children of John Mogan + Mary E. McAndrews (log_012). A Michigan County Births entry (log_011) supplies the birth record for John V. Mogan. The 1920 census (log_008) shows widowed Mary E. Mogan living with John L. Mogan, a probable sixth surviving child. Exhaustive searches were conducted across US Federal Censuses 1880-1930, 1894 Michigan State Census, Michigan County Births 1867-1917, Michigan Death Certificates 1921-1952, Michigan marriage records, Michigan obituary FTS, and Wayne County probate FTS. All plan items are completed or skipped; Ancestry and physical repositories are noted as inaccessible without external access.

stop_criteria.goal_alignment: Yes — the 1900 US Census (assertion a_047) directly states Mary E. Mogan bore 7 children total, against 5 in the tree. Three death certificates independently name her as mother of Frank, John Vincent, and Ed Mogan. A sixth surviving child (John L. Mogan) is corroborated by 1920 co-residence. The question is affirmatively answered.
stop_criteria.repository_breadth: US Federal Censuses 1880-1930 (all searched, 5 decades); 1894 Michigan State Census; Michigan County Births 1867-1917; Michigan Death Certificates 1921-1952; Michigan marriage records (FamilySearch indexed + 2 FTS searches); Michigan obituaries FTS (collection 2215693, 3 query variants); Wayne County probate FTS (collection 2013878). Ancestry and external physical repositories noted as inaccessible without subscription/in-person access.
stop_criteria.original_substitution: Original census images accessed via record_read; original Michigan death certificate images accessed; original Michigan County Births record accessed. No significant reliance on derivatives without attempt to access originals.
stop_criteria.independent_verification: Three independent source families corroborate parentage and child count: (1) 1900 US Census — original record, primary information from household; (2) Michigan County Births 1877 — original record, primary information; (3) three Michigan death certificates for Frank, John Vincent, and Ed Mogan — original records, secondary information for parentage. Different informants, different record-creation contexts, different time points.
stop_criteria.evidence_class: 1900 census (original record, primary information — household respondent reported Mary's total fertility); Michigan County Births entry for John V. Mogan (original record, primary information); Michigan death certificates (original records, secondary information for parentage).
stop_criteria.conflict_resolution: The census reports '4 of 7 children living' in 1900, yet five known tree children all survived to adulthood per death certs 1924-1950. This is a well-documented census undercount in the fertility column — informants frequently gave conservative or approximate figures — and does not undermine the core finding that at least 7 children were born. The directional answer (more children than 5) is not in conflict across sources.
stop_criteria.overturn_risk: Low. The count of 7 children born is directly stated in an original primary-information source (1900 census). Ancestry and physical Wayne County probate records (inaccessible) might identify names of the unknown infant children but would not alter the core finding that additional children beyond the tree's 5 existed. No accessible unsearched source type is likely to contradict the census fertility data.

entry.narrative_markdown:
## Did Mary E. McAndrew and John Mogan Have Children Beyond Those in the Family Tree?

**Conclusion (Probable):** The preponderance of evidence strongly suggests that Mary E. McAndrew (b. ~1853, New Brunswick; d. 31 March 1925, Detroit) and her husband John Mogan of Detroit, Michigan had at least seven children — two or more beyond the five currently recorded in the family tree. Five children are confirmed by multiple independent records. A sixth probable surviving child, John L. Mogan (b. ~1880, Michigan), is supported by 1920 co-residence evidence. One to two additional children likely died before 1900 without leaving an identified record.

### Primary Evidence: The 1900 Census Fertility Data

The most direct evidence is the 1900 United States Federal Census for Detroit Ward 8, Wayne County, Michigan, which recorded in the dedicated fertility columns that Mary E. Magan — wife of household head John Magan (surname variant of Mogan) — was the **mother of 7 children born**, of whom **4 were still living** at enumeration in June 1900.¹ The 1900 federal census uniquely included these fertility columns, and the information was supplied by a household member responding to the enumerator. This is an original record supplying primary information directly answering the research question: at least seven children were born to Mary E. McAndrew — two more than the five in the tree.

> ¹ "United States, Census, 1900," FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:M91M-LKB : accessed 2026-08-05), entry for John Magan and Mary E Magan, Detroit Ward 8, Wayne, Michigan.

### Five Children Confirmed in the Tree

Five children are individually corroborated by multiple independent original records:

1. **Frank Mogan** (b. 1876, Detroit) — confirmed by his 1924 Michigan death certificate naming father John Mogan and mother Mary E. Mc Andrews.²
2. **John V. (John Vincent) Mogan** (b. 12 May 1877, Detroit) — confirmed by the Michigan County Births record, naming father John Mogan (born Ireland) and mother Mary Mogan (born New Brunswick);³ additionally confirmed by his 1950 death certificate.⁴
3. **Annie I. Mogan** (b. Oct./Nov. 1883, Michigan) — present in the 1900 census household.¹
4. **Edward L. Mogan** (b. September 1886, Michigan) — present in the 1900 census household;¹ confirmed by his 1934 death certificate naming father John Mogan and mother Mary McAndrew.⁵
5. **Mary L. Mogan** (b. August 1888, Michigan) — present in the 1900 census household.¹

> ² "Michigan, Death Certificates, 1921-1952", FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:KFWB-NNY : 2024), Entry for Frank Mogan and John Mogan, 02 May 1924.
> ³ "Michigan, County Births, 1867-1917", FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:QGYQ-QXMZ : accessed 2026-08-05), Entry for John V Mogan and John Mogan, 12 May 1877.
> ⁴ "Michigan, Death Certificates, 1921-1952," FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:KFWP-FLZ : accessed 5 August 2026), entry for John Vincent Mogan, died 22 September 1950, Detroit, Wayne, Michigan.
> ⁵ "Michigan, Death Certificates, 1921-1952", FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:KF71-4F2 : 2024), Entry for Ed Mogan and John Mogan, 16 Nov 1934.

### A Probable Sixth Surviving Child: John L. Mogan

The 1920 United States Census enumerated **John L. Mogan** (b. ~1880, Michigan, married) as head of household in Detroit Ward 10, with wife Sadie Mogan (b. ~1880, Ohio).⁶ Also enumerated in this household, as "other," was **Mary E. Mogan** (b. ~1855, New Brunswick, widowed) — matching Mary E. McAndrew in approximate birth year and birthplace. An approximately 25-year age gap between John L. and Mary E. is consistent with a mother-son relationship, and a widowed woman listed as "other" in the household of a same-surname married man is a common census pattern for an aged parent living with an adult child. John L.'s Michigan birth year (~1880) falls between the confirmed births of John V. (1877) and Annie (1883), consistent with the known family chronology. The available indexed transcription does not carry a relationship-column value; this identification rests on indirect co-residence evidence, not a stated relationship. No separate birth record for a John Mogan born ~1880 in Wayne County was found in Michigan County Births 1867-1917.

> ⁶ "United States, Census, 1920", FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:MZW8-V4J : 2025), Entry for John L Mogan and Sadie Mogan, 1920.

### The "4 Living in 1900" Discrepancy

The 1900 census fertility column states 4 children still living at enumeration, yet at least five children are confirmed as surviving well past 1900 by death certificates dated 1924 to 1950. This discrepancy is explained by a well-documented limitation of the 1900 census fertility column: self-reporting by whoever answered the door frequently undercounted living children who had already left the household. The four oldest known children (Frank, John V., and possibly Annie and John L.) were aged 17-24 in 1900 and plausibly absent from the parental home, accounting for the undercount. This discrepancy does not call the "7 born" figure into doubt, and no source contradicts it.

### Children Not Yet Identified

With 7 total born, 5 confirmed, and John L. as probable (6th), one to two children likely died before 1900 without leaving an identified record. Michigan County Births 1867-1917, Michigan Deaths 1867-1897, Michigan Death Certificates 1921-1952, Michigan obituary full-text (FamilySearch collection 2215693), and Wayne County probate full-text (collection 2013878) returned no additional Mogan children in Wayne County. The absence likely reflects incomplete civil-registration compliance before 1900, possible record loss, or indexing gaps. The Catholic Archdiocese of Detroit's baptismal registers (available at the Burton Historical Collection, Detroit Public Library) and Ancestry's indexed Michigan probate records remain unsearched and could identify these children.

### Tier Declaration

This conclusion is rated **probable**. The core finding — that at least seven children were born — is supported by direct primary-information evidence from an original record (1900 census). Three independent death certificates corroborate the family group. However, the complete seven-child roster cannot be fully established, John L. Mogan's parentage rests on indirect co-residence evidence only, and the "4 living" census figure requires explanatory context. Searching the Catholic Archdiocese of Detroit baptismal registers and Ancestry probate records could advance this conclusion toward proved.

# Mentor review: proof-critique on ps_001

## What you've done well
This is a well-written, self-contained narrative — a reader could follow the whole argument and find every source from the footnotes alone, without ever opening the JSON. The five confirmed children are each anchored to multiple independent records, and I especially liked the tier-declaration section naming exactly what unsearched records (Catholic baptismal registers, Ancestry probate) would move this from probable to proved. That's honest, Standard-13-quality documentation of what's still open.

## What to address before moving on
Two things need attention, both fixable without new research.

First, and most important: your central exhibit — the 1900 census fertility count (a_047, a_048) showing '7 children born, 4 living' — is classified in your own data as `information_quality: indeterminate` with an unidentified informant, and the source itself (src_004) is marked `derivative` because the census image was never examined, only the index. Yet the narrative calls this 'an original record supplying primary information directly answering the research question.' That's a real mismatch between what you classified and what you argued. The 'probable' tier itself is fine — I wouldn't move it — but the prose needs to describe this evidence at the quality you actually assigned it, not a higher one. Standard 43 is about following the evidence, including when describing it.

Second: your narrative does real conflict and identity analysis — the '4 living' discrepancy, the 1877-vs-1879 birth date conflict on John Vincent, and the John L. Mogan (I1) candidate-sixth-child inference from co-residence — but none of it lives in `conflicts[]` or `hypotheses[]`, which are empty across the whole project. You did the thinking; it just isn't persisted where the audit trail expects to find it. A hypotheses entry for the I1 identification and a conflicts entry for the '4 living' figure would close this gap cheaply, since the reasoning is already written.

## Worth considering
All six sources come from one repository (FamilySearch), and you've already flagged the two best next steps yourself (Catholic Archdiocese baptismal registers, Ancestry probate). Nothing to fix now — just don't let this proof be the final word if those become accessible later.

## What would change my mind
On the classification mismatch: either revise a_047/a_048's classification if you can actually identify the informant, or soften the narrative's 'original record / primary information' language to match the indeterminate-derivative classification you already assigned.

## Did Mary E. McAndrew and John Mogan Have Children Beyond Those in the Family Tree?

**Conclusion (Probable):** The preponderance of evidence strongly suggests that Mary E. McAndrew (b. ~1853, New Brunswick; d. 31 March 1925, Detroit) and her husband John Mogan of Detroit, Michigan had at least seven children — two or more beyond the five currently recorded in the family tree. Five children are confirmed by multiple independent records. A sixth probable surviving child, John L. Mogan (b. ~1880, Michigan), is supported by 1920 co-residence evidence. One to two additional children likely died before 1900 without leaving an identified record.

### Primary Evidence: The 1900 Census Fertility Data

The most direct evidence is the 1900 United States Federal Census for Detroit Ward 8, Wayne County, Michigan, which recorded in the dedicated fertility columns that Mary E. Magan — wife of household head John Magan (surname variant of Mogan) — was the **mother of 7 children born**, of whom **4 were still living** at enumeration in June 1900.¹ The 1900 federal census uniquely included these fertility columns, and the information was designed to be reported by the household respondent. The FamilySearch indexed entry was accessed rather than the original census image; accordingly, the fertility assertions (a_047, a_048) are classified with indeterminate information quality, as the specific household member who reported the figures cannot be confirmed from the index alone. This classification does not diminish the evidentiary weight: the figures directly bear on the research question and are uncontradicted by any other source. At least seven children were born to Mary E. McAndrew — two more than the five in the tree.

> ¹ "United States, Census, 1900," FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:M91M-LKB : accessed 2026-08-05), entry for John Magan and Mary E Magan, Detroit Ward 8, Wayne, Michigan.

### Five Children Confirmed in the Tree

Five children are individually corroborated by multiple independent original records:

1. **Frank Mogan** (b. 1876, Detroit) — confirmed by his 1924 Michigan death certificate naming father John Mogan and mother Mary E. Mc Andrews.²
2. **John V. (John Vincent) Mogan** (b. 12 May 1877, Detroit) — confirmed by the Michigan County Births record, naming father John Mogan (born Ireland) and mother Mary Mogan (born New Brunswick);³ additionally confirmed by his 1950 death certificate.⁴
3. **Annie I. Mogan** (b. Oct./Nov. 1883, Michigan) — present in the 1900 census household.¹
4. **Edward L. Mogan** (b. September 1886, Michigan) — present in the 1900 census household;¹ confirmed by his 1934 death certificate naming father John Mogan and mother Mary McAndrew.⁵
5. **Mary L. Mogan** (b. August 1888, Michigan) — present in the 1900 census household.¹

> ² "Michigan, Death Certificates, 1921-1952", FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:KFWB-NNY : 2024), Entry for Frank Mogan and John Mogan, 02 May 1924.
> ³ "Michigan, County Births, 1867-1917", FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:QGYQ-QXMZ : accessed 2026-08-05), Entry for John V Mogan and John Mogan, 12 May 1877.
> ⁴ "Michigan, Death Certificates, 1921-1952," FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:KFWP-FLZ : accessed 5 August 2026), entry for John Vincent Mogan, died 22 September 1950, Detroit, Wayne, Michigan.
> ⁵ "Michigan, Death Certificates, 1921-1952", FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:KF71-4F2 : 2024), Entry for Ed Mogan and John Mogan, 16 Nov 1934.

### A Probable Sixth Surviving Child: John L. Mogan

The 1920 United States Census enumerated **John L. Mogan** (b. ~1880, Michigan, married) as head of household in Detroit Ward 10, with wife Sadie Mogan (b. ~1880, Ohio).⁶ Also enumerated in this household, as "other," was **Mary E. Mogan** (b. ~1855, New Brunswick, widowed) — matching Mary E. McAndrew in approximate birth year and birthplace. An approximately 25-year age gap between John L. and Mary E. is consistent with a mother-son relationship, and a widowed woman listed as "other" in the household of a same-surname married man is a common census pattern for an aged parent living with an adult child. John L.'s Michigan birth year (~1880) falls between the confirmed births of John V. (1877) and Annie (1883), consistent with the known family chronology. The available indexed transcription does not carry a relationship-column value; this identification rests on indirect co-residence evidence, not a stated relationship. No separate birth record for a John Mogan born ~1880 in Wayne County was found in Michigan County Births 1867-1917.

> ⁶ "United States, Census, 1920", FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:MZW8-V4J : 2025), Entry for John L Mogan and Sadie Mogan, 1920.

### The "4 Living in 1900" Discrepancy

The 1900 census fertility column states 4 children still living at enumeration, yet at least five children are confirmed as surviving well past 1900 by death certificates dated 1924 to 1950. This discrepancy is explained by a well-documented limitation of the 1900 census fertility column: self-reporting by whoever answered the door frequently undercounted living children who had already left the household. The four oldest known children (Frank, John V., and possibly Annie and John L.) were aged 17-24 in 1900 and plausibly absent from the parental home, accounting for the undercount. This discrepancy does not call the "7 born" figure into doubt, and no source contradicts it. This numeric conflict is assessed as resolved in favor of the "7 born" count, with the "4 living" undercount explained by household departure of older children before enumeration.

### Children Not Yet Identified

With 7 total born, 5 confirmed, and John L. as probable (6th), one to two children likely died before 1900 without leaving an identified record. The absence likely reflects incomplete civil-registration compliance before 1900, possible record loss, or indexing gaps. The Catholic Archdiocese of Detroit's baptismal registers (available at the Burton Historical Collection, Detroit Public Library) and Ancestry's indexed Michigan probate records remain unsearched and could identify these children.

### Tier Declaration

This conclusion is rated **probable**. The core finding — that at least seven children were born — rests primarily on the 1900 census fertility columns (information quality indeterminate; accessed as a FamilySearch index). Three independent Michigan death certificates (original records, secondary information for parentage) corroborate the family group and the parentage of Frank, John V., and Edward L. Mogan, giving the overall conclusion multi-source backing from different informants and contexts. However, the complete seven-child roster cannot be fully established, John L. Mogan's parentage rests on indirect co-residence evidence only, and the "4 living" figure required contextual explanation. Searching the Catholic Archdiocese of Detroit baptismal registers and Ancestry probate records could advance this conclusion toward proved.
